def fib_fast(n, f0 = 0, f1 = 1) -> int:
    """
    iteratively solves a recurrence that performs matrix exponentiation
    """
    a, b = 0, 1
    for bit in f"{n:b}":
        a, b = (a + 2 * b) * a, a * a + b * b
        if bit == "1":
            a, b = a + b, a
    return a * f1 + b * f0

    result = func(n)

def writing_as_sum(n):
    if n <= 0: return [[]]
    out = []
    for i in range(n, 0, -1):
        for l in writing_as_sum(n - i):

Definition 1 (Matching) 
A matching in an undireted graph is an edge set such that every vertex belongs to either one (matched vertex) or \(\emptyset\) (free vertex) edges of the matching.

Maximum Matching Problem. Given a graph \(G\), find a matching with as many edges as possible.
We start by considering a natural question: given a graph \(G\) and a suboptimal matching \(M\), how should we improve it? Answering this leads to a natural iterative mechanism for producing the maximum matching.
We start by introducing structures in the graph that correspond to ways in which we may alter our matching.

Definition 2 (Alternating Component) 
An \(M\)-alternating component is an edge set that forms a connected subgraph of \(G\) of maximum degree \(2\), in which every degree-\(2\) vertex belongs to exactly one edge of \(M\).

A connected subgraph of \(G\) of maximum degree \(2\) must be either a cycle or a path. It is a cycle iff every vertex has degree \(2\). A proof for this can be furnished by considering the longest path in the subgraph.

Definition 3 (\(M\)-Augmenting Path) 
Suppose \(G\) is a graph and \(M\) is a matching. Then, an \(M\)-augmenting path in \(G\) is a path \(P\) in \(G\) that starts and ends at free vertices and alternates between edges in \(M\) and not in \(M\).

The following are some easy but useful properties of an \(M\)-augmenting path.

Lemma 1 (Properties of \(M\)-Augmenting Paths) 
Let \(P\) be an \(M\)-augmenting path. Then

\(P\) has odd length;
\(|P \backslash M| = |M \cap P| + 1.\)



Proof. 

Let \(P = v_0 v_1 \dots v_k\). Then \(v_i v_{ i + 1 } \in M\) iff \(i \equiv 1 \; (\mathrm{mod} \; 2)\). As \(v_k\) is free, we have \(v_{ k - 1 } v_k \notin M\) which implies \((k - 1) \equiv 0 \; (\mathrm{mod} \; 2)\) so that \(\ell(P) = k \equiv 1 \; (\mathrm{mod} \; 2)\).
Let \(P = v_0 v_1 \dots v_k\). It suffices to show that \(P' = v_0 v_1 \dots v_{ k - 1 }\) is such that \(|P' \backslash M| = |P' \cap M|\). For this just consider the \(P' \cap M \rightarrow P' \backslash M\) bijection defined by \(v_i v_{ i + 1 } \rightarrow v_{ i - 1 } v_i\).


The following result then demonstrates how the presence of a suitable \(M\)-alternating component allows us to alter our matching. Informally, by suitable, we want the alternating component to “never lose track of already matched vertices”– that is the alternating component can contain a vertex from the matching only if it contains the edge the vertex is matched to too.

Proposition 1 (Augmenting by an \(M\)-Alternating Component) 
Suppose \(C\) is an \(M\)-alternating component such that \(v \in V(M) \cap V(C) \implies v \in V(M \cap C)\). Then, \(M \oplus C\) is a matching such that \[|M \oplus C| = |M| + |C \backslash M| - |M \cap C|.\]


Proof. 
We first show that \(M \oplus C\) is a matching. Consider a vertex \(v \in M \oplus C\). It suffices to prove that \(v\) is adjacent to exactly one edge of \(M \oplus C\). Note that \(M \oplus C = (M \backslash C) \sqcup (C \backslash M)\). Note that \(M \backslash C\) is a matching as \(M\) is a matching. Furthermore, \(C \backslash M\) is a matching since every \(v \in V(C \backslash M)\) is adjacent to exactly one edge in \(C \backslash M\). So, it suffices to show that \(M \backslash C\) and \(C \backslash M\) are vertex disjoint. If \(v \in V(M \backslash C)\) then there is a unique \(e \in M\) such that \(v \in e\). Note that \(e \notin M \cap C\) and so \(v \notin V(C)\).
Thus, \[\begin{align*}
|M \oplus C| &= |(M \backslash C) \sqcup (C \backslash M)| \\ &= |M \backslash C| + |C \backslash M| \\ &= |M| + |C \backslash M| - |M \cap C|.
\end{align*}\]

Consequently, an \(M\)-augmenting path is an alternating component that increases the size of the matching.

Corollary 1 (Augmenting by an \(M\)-Augmenting Path) 
If \(P\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path then \(M \oplus P\) is a matching and \(|M \oplus P| = |M| + 1\). Furthermore, every vertex matched in \(M\) is also matched in \(M \oplus P\).


Proof. 
Note that if \(v \in V(P) \cap V(M)\) then by definition of an \(M\)-augmenting path \(v\) must be an interior vertex that is adjacent to an edge in \(M \cap P\). Thus, \(M \oplus P\) is a matching. Furthermore, as \(|P \backslash M| = |M \cap P| + 1\) we have \(|M \oplus P| = |M| + 1\).
Now, we show \(V(M) \subseteq V(M \oplus P)\). Suppose \(v \in M\). Note that if \(v \notin P\), then clearly \(v \in M \backslash P \subseteq M \oplus P\). Otherwise, \(v \in P\) and as \(v\) is not \(M\)-free, it must be an interior vertex that is adjacent to an edge in \(P \backslash M\) which implies \(v \in P \backslash M \subseteq M \oplus P\).

In fact, \(M\)-alternating components completely characterize the maximum matching problem.

Lemma 2 (Changes in Matching I) 
If \(M\) and \(M'\) are matchings in \(G\) then \(M \oplus M'\) is a union of \(M\)-alternating components.


Proof. 
Every \(v \in M \oplus M'\) has degree \(\in \{1, 2\}\) as every vertex has degree at most \(1\) in each of \(M, M'\), with degree \(1\) in at least one or the other. Furthermore, a vertex \(v \in M \oplus M'\) can only be adjacent to at most one edge in \(M\) as \(M\) is a matching. Thus, \(M \oplus M'\) is a union of \(M\)-alternating components.


Lemma 3 (Changes in Matching II) 
If \(M\) and \(M'\) are matchings in \(G\) with \(|M| < |M'|\) then \(M \oplus M'\) contains an \(M\)-augmenting path.


Proof. 
\(M \oplus M'\) is a union of \(M\)-alternating components. An \(M\)-alternating component where all vertices have degree-\(2\) must be a cycle. Since the edges must alternate between edges in \(M\) and in \(M'\), the cycle must have an equal number of edges from \(M\) and \(M'\). Since \(|M| < |M'|\) we must then have an \(M\)-alternating component that is a path and contains more edges from \(M'\) than \(M\).

This motivates a family of algorithms for the maximum matching problem.


\begin{algorithm} \caption{Computing a Maximum-Matching} \begin{algorithmic} \State{\textbf{initialize} $M = \emptyset$} \Repeat \State{$P \leftarrow$ \textbf{find} an $M$-augmenting path} \State{$M \leftarrow M \oplus P$} \Until{there is no $M$-augmenting path} \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


This algorithm terminates in at most \(\mathcal{O}(n/2)\) iterations as each iteration increases the size of the matching by \(1\) and a maximum matching has size at most \(n/2\).
Different strategies for finding the \(M\)-augmenting path \(P\) yield different algorithms.

Definition 4 (Bipartite) 
A graph \(G\) is said to be bipartite if there exists a partition \(V(G) = L \sqcup R\) such that every edge has exactly one endpoint in \(L\) and \(R\).

We now present a simple strategy that works when \(G\) is bipartite.

Definition 5 (\(G_M\)) 
Let \(G=(L, R, E)\) be a bipartite graph and \(M\) be a matching. The graph \(G_M\) is defined as the directed graph formed from \(G\) by orienting each edge from \(L\) to \(R\) if it does not belong to \(M\) and from \(L\) to \(R\), otherwise.


Lemma 4 
Let \(M\) be a matching in a bipartite graph \(G\) and \(F\) be the set of free vertices. The \(M\)-augmenting paths are in one-to-one correspondence with directed paths from \(L \cap F\) to \(R \cap F\) in \(G_M\).


Proof. 
Let \(P\) be a directed path from \(L \cap F\) to \(R \cap F\) in \(G_M\). First, its endpoints are free with respect to \(M\). Since \(G_M\) is bipartite, its edges alternate from edges \(L \to R\) and edges \(R \to L\). That is, the edges alternate from edges in \(M\) and not in \(M\). Thus, the undirected edge set corresponding to \(P\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path.
Next, let \(P\) be an augmenting path. Note that \(P\) has odd length, and hence, its endpoints are on opposite sides of the partition \((L, R)\). Since its endpoints are also free, it suffices to show that \(P\) corresponds to a directed path in \(G_M\). Note that every interior vertex of \(P\) has exactly one edge in \(M\) and one edge not in \(M\). The former edge corresponds to a directed edge \(R \to L\) and the latter corresponds to a directed edge \(L \to R\). Thus, \(P\) corresponds to a directed path in \(G_M\) from \(L \cap F\) and \(R \cap F\).

This gives us a natural algorithm for maximum-matching in a bipartite graph. We merely build \(G_M\) and find a path from \(L \cap F\) to \(R \cap F\) using BFS/DFS. Building \(G_M\) and performing BFS/DFS both take \(\mathcal{O}(m + n)\) time. We may also assume \(m \ge n/2\); otherwise, the graph contains isolated edges which can be removed in a preprocessing step taking \(\mathcal{ O }(n)\) times. Thus, overall, we get a \(\mathcal{ O }(m n)\) algorithm for maximum-matching in bipartite graphs.



Choosing only one augmenting path at a time is quite wasteful. The Hopcroft-Karp algorithm improves upon this by attempting to find many disjoint augmenting paths in every iteration. We start with the following generalization of Corollary 1 and Lemma 3.
As a brief aside, vertex disjoint may refer to different notions depending on the source.

Definition 6 (Vertex Disjoint) 
A set of subgraphs \(\{G_i\}\) are (externally) vertex-disjoint if they share no vertices. A set of paths \(\{P_i\}\) are said to be internally vertex-disjoint if they share no vertices other than their endpoints.


Lemma 5 (Characterization of Augmentable Matchings) 
If \(G\) is a graph and \(M\) is a matching \(G\) then the following are equivalent for all \(k \in \mathbb{N}\)

there exists a matching \(M'\) with \(|M| + k\) edges;
\(G\) contains \(k\) vertex-disjoint \(M\)-augmenting paths;
there exists a matching \(M'\) such that the edge set \(M \oplus M'\) contains at least \(k\) vertex-disjoint \(M\)-augmenting paths.



Proof. 

\(a. \Rightarrow c.\)

Consider \(M'\) such that \(|M'| = |M| + k\). Note that \(M \oplus M' = (M \backslash M') \sqcup (M' \backslash M)\) with \(|M' \backslash M| = |M \backslash M'| + k\). Every vertex \(v \in M \oplus M'\) has degree \(\in \{1, 2\}\) as every vertex has degree at most \(1\) in each of \(M\), \(M'\) and degree \(1\) in at least one of \(M\), \(M'\). Thus, \(M \oplus M'\) must be a union of vertex-disjoint paths and cycles.
As \(M\) and \(M'\) are matchings, each vertex of degree \(2\) in \(M \oplus M'\) is adjacent to exactly one edge from \(M\) and one edge from \(M'\). Since a cycle can be alternating only if it has even length, it has an equal number of edges from \(M\) and \(M'\). Since \(|M' \backslash M| = |M \backslash M'| + k\), there must be at least \(k\)-many \(M\)-alternating paths in \(M \oplus M'\).

\(c. \Rightarrow b.\)

This is immediate by noting that \(M \oplus M' \subseteq E(G)\).

\(b. \Rightarrow a.\)

It suffices to show that if \(P\) and \(P'\) are vertex disjoint \(M\)-augmenting paths then \(P'\) is also a \((M \oplus P)\)-augmenting path. As \(P\) and \(P'\) are vertex-disjoint, they are edge disjoint too. Since endpoints of \(P'\) aren’t adjacent to edges in \(M\) or \(P\), they will be free with respect to \(M \oplus P\) too. Next, any edge of \(M \cap P' \subseteq M \\ P\) is still in \(M \oplus P\). Furthermore, any edge of \(P' \backslash M\) isn’t contained in \(M\) or \(P\) and hence, isn’t an edge in \(M \oplus P\). Thus, \(P'\) is \((M \oplus P)\)-alternating.

Again, we shall assume \(G\) is bipartite. As always, we start with some helpful definitions to frame our algorithm.

Definition 7 (BFS Levels) 
In the graph \(G_M\), define \(L_0, L_1, ..., L_\infty\) to be the levels in a breadth-first traversal rooted at \(L \cap F\). That is,
\[\begin{align*}
L_0 = & L \cap F, \\ L_{i + 1} = &\text{ all vertices } v \notin \bigcup_{ k = 0 }^i L_k \text{ s.t. } G_M \\ &\text{ contains an edge from } L_i \text{ to } v, \\ L_\infty = &\text{ all vertices} v \notin \bigcup_{k = 1}^n L_k.
\end{align*}\]


Definition 8 (Advancing and Retreating Edges) 
An edge \(e = (u, v) \in G_M\) is an advancing edge if \(u \in L_i\) and \(v \in L_{i + 1}\). Otherwise, we call it a retreating edge. A path composed entirely of advancing edges is called an advancing path.

The following lemma then somewhat clarifies the importance of advancing edges.

Lemma 6 
If \(e = (u, v)\) is an advancing edge we must have \(d(v) > d(u) \Rightarrow d(v) = d(u) + 1\). Consequently, an \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\) is an advancing path if and only if it is a shortest \(s\)-\(t\) path.


Proof. 
By definition, if \(e\) is an edge going from \(L_i\) to \(L_j\) for \(j > i\), then we must have \(j = i + 1\). Furthermore, \(L_i\) consists of all vertices that are at a distance of \(i\) from \(L_0\).


Definition 9 (Blocking Set) 
A blocking set of \(M\)-augmenting paths is a maximal (under set-inclusion) set of vertex-disjoint advancing \(M\)-augmenting paths.



\begin{algorithm} \caption{Hopcroft-Karp Algorithm} \begin{algorithmic} \State{\textbf{initialize} $M = \emptyset$} \Repeat \State{$\{P_i\} \leftarrow$ \textbf{find} a blocking set of $M$-augmenting paths} \State{$M \leftarrow M \oplus P_1 \oplus \dots P_k$} \Until{there is no $M$-augmenting path} \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


As before, we know that this algorithm terminates in at most \(n/2\) iterations as each iteration increases the cardinality of \(M\) by at least \(1\). To obtain a superior bound, we need to also integrate an alternative measure of progress. Particularly, we shall show that the length of the shortest augmenting path is strictly increasing every iteration. Intuitively, this occurs because augmenting by a path reverses the orientation of all its edges and hence, any future \(s\)-\(t\) path taking these edges must be longer than the shortest \(s\)-\(t\) paths available prior.

Lemma 7 (Increasing Augmenting Path Lengths) 
If \(M_t\) and \(M_{ t + 1 }\) are the matchings in two consecutive iterations of the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm, the length of the shortest \(M_{ t + 1 }\)-augmenting path is strictly greater than the length of the shortest \(M_t\)-augmenting path.

Our strategy will be to “follow” along a path \(P\) in \(G_{M_{t + 1}}\) while keeping track of the distances as we would in \(G_{M_t}\)! Note that the undirected edge structure of both \(G_{M_t}\) and \(G_{M_{t + 1}}\) are identical, the only distinction lie in the orientation of an edge and the BFS layers. The latter is really a consequence of the former: the availibility of directed edges is what changes the shortest path. Furthermore, the notion of advancing and retreating edges help us compare the path \(P\) in \(G_{M_{t + 1}}\) to the shortest paths in \(G_{M_t}\).

Proof. 
Let \(L_0, L_1, \dots,\) denote the BFS layers of \(G_{ M_t }\) and suppose \(d \in \mathbb{N}\) is minimal such that \(L_d\) intersects \(R \cap F\). Furthermore, suppose \(P = u_0 u_1 \dots u_j\) is a shortest \(M_{ t + 1 }\)-augmenting path. Note that \(u_0, u_j\) must be free with respect to \(M_t\) as once a vertex is matched, it remains matched after augementation too. Below \(d(\cdot)\) denotes the distance in \(G_{ M_t }\) from \(L \cap F\). Edges \((u_i, u_{ i + 1 })\) were either:

advancing edges in \(G_{M_t}\) whose orientation is reversed in \(G_{M_{t + 1}}\) (because \((u_{i + 1}, u_i)\) belonged to a blocking set \(\mathcal{ P }\)) \[ d(u_{ i }) = d(u_{ i + 1 }) + 1, \]
advancing edges in \(G_{M_t}\) whose orientation is preserved in \(G_{M_{t + 1}}\) \[ d(u_{ i + 1 }) = d(u_i) + 1, \]
reversing edges in \(G_{M_t}\) \[ d(u_{ i + 1 }) < d(u_i). \] Thus, in all cases we have \(d(u_{ i + 1 }) \le d(u_i) + 1\). Inductively, \(d \le d(u_j) \le j\).

Note that \(d(u_j) = j\) if and only if \(P\) is an advancing path in \(G_{M_t}\). This implies that \(P\) is edge disjoint from the blocking set of \(M_{t}\)-augmenting paths, \(M_t \oplus M_{ t + 1 }\). Since \(P\) wasn’t used as an augmenting path in iteration \(t\), it must be the case that there exists \(v \in V(M_t \oplus M_{ t + 1 }) \cap V(P)\). Since all vertices in \(V(M_t \oplus M_{t+1})\) are matched in \(M_{t+1}\), vertex \(v\) cannot be an endpoint of \(P\) (which are \(M_{t+1}\)-free). Since \(M_t \oplus M_{t + 1}\) is a blocking set, each vertex therein is adjacent to an edge \(e \in M_{t + 1} \backslash M_t\).
As \(P\) is \(M_{ t + 1 }\)-augmenting and \(v\) is an interior vertex of \(P\), the unique edge of \(M_{ t + 1 }\) adjacent to \(v\), namely \(e\), is contained in \(P\). That is, \(e \in (M_t \backslash M_{ t + 1 }) \cap P\), contradicting the edge-disjointness of \(P\) from \(M_t \oplus M_{ t + 1 }\).
Thus, \(d \le d(u_j) < j\).

Note that as augmenting paths are of odd length, each iteration increases the length of the shortest \(M\)-augmenting path by at least two. Using these measures of progress independently, we get the same bound of \(n/2\) on the number of iterations. Using these two measures in different phases of the algorithm yields a superior bound than using either one alone.

Proposition 2 (Hopcroft-Karp Iterations) 
For any \(t \le n/2\), the number of iterations of Hopcraft-Karp is bounded by \(t + n/2t\).


Proof. 
After \(t\) iterations, the length of the shortest \(M\)-augmenting path is at least \(2 t\). Then let \(k = |M^\star| - |M_t|\). Note that \(M\) must have at least one augmenting path with vertices at most \(n/k\). Hence, \(2 t \le n/k \Rightarrow k \le n/(2t)\). Thus, the runtime is bounded by \(t + k \le t + n/(2t)\).

By the AM-GM inequality, we note that \(\sqrt{ 2 n } \le t + n/2t\) with equality obtained when \(t = \sqrt{n/2}\).

Corollary 2 
Hopcroft-Karp terminates in at most \(\mathcal{ O }(\sqrt{ n })\) iterations.




Minimum-Cost Bipartite Perfect Matching. Given an undirected bipartite graph \(G = (L, R, E)\) together with costs \(c: E \to \mathbb{R}_{ \ge 0 }\) for each edge, find a perfect matching \(M\) that minimizes \(c(M) = \sum_{ e \in M } c(e)\).
Without loss of generality, we shall assume that a perfect matching exists as we have already discussed algorithms capable of detecting this.

Definition 10 (Induced Costs) 
Let \(M\) be a matching. Then \(c: E \to \mathbb{R}_{ \ge 0 }\) induces a cost function \(c_M: E \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \[ c_M (e) = \Bbb{1}\{e \notin M\} \cdot c(e) - \Bbb{1}\{e \in M\} \cdot c(e). \]

This induced cost is natural for \(M\)-augmenting paths due to the following lemma.

Lemma 8 (Costs Under Augmentation) 
If \(P\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path then \[ c(M \oplus P) = c(M) + c_M (P).\]

This motivates a greedy algorithm for our problem. Note that bipartiteness is not required yet.


\begin{algorithm} \caption{Greedy Algorithm for Min-Cost Perfect Matching} \begin{algorithmic} \State{\textbf{initialize} $M = \emptyset$} \While{$M$ is not a perfect matching} \State{$P \leftarrow$ \textbf{find} an $M$-augmenting path minimizing $c_M(\cdot)$} \State{$M \leftarrow M \oplus P$} \EndWhile \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


Correctness follows from a proof by induction showing that at iteration \(t\), we have the minimum-cost matching of cardinality \(t\).

Lemma 9 (Correctness) 
If \(M_k\) is a minimum-cost matching of size \(k\) in \(G\) and \(P\) is an \(M_k\)-augmenting path of minimum incremental cost, then \(M_k \oplus P\) is a minimum-cost matching of size \(k + 1\).


Proof. 
Let \(M_{ k + 1 }\) denote the minimum-cost matching of size \(k + 1\). By definition, we must have \(c(M_{ k + 1 }) \le c(M_k \oplus P)\).
Now, we prove the reverse inequality. \(M_k \oplus M_{ k + 1 }\) is a union of alternating components that must contain at least one \(M_k\)-alternating path \(Q\) as \(|M_{ k + 1 }| = |M_k| + 1\). Let \(R\) denote the union of the remaining alternating components. Note that \(R\) must have the same number of edges in \(M_k\) and in \(M_{ k + 1 }\) since the path \(Q\) already accounts for \(|M_{ k + 1 }| = |M_k| + 1\). So, \(M_k \oplus R\) is a \(k\)-matching and \(M_{ k + 1 } \oplus R\) is a \((k + 1)\)-matching. From this, it is immediate that \(c_{M_k} (R), c_{M_{ k + 1 }}(R) \ge 0\) via \[\begin{align*}
c(M_k) \le c(M_k \oplus R) = c(M_k) + c_{ M_k }(R) \\ c(M_{ k + 1 }) \le c(M_{ k + 1 } \oplus R) = c(M_{ k + 1 }) + c_{ M_{ k + 1 } }(R).
\end{align*}\]
Furthermore, we have \(c_{ M_k }(R) + c_{ M_{ k + 1 } }(R) = 0\) which implies \(c_{ M_k }(R) = c_{ M_{ k + 1 } }(R) = 0\). \[\begin{align*}
c_{ M_k }(R) + c_{ M_{ k + 1 } }(R) &= c(R \backslash M_k) - c(R \cap M_k) + c(R \backslash M_{ k + 1 }) - c(R \cap M_{ k + 1 }) \\ &= c(R \cap M_{ k + 1 }) - c(R \cap M_k) + c(R \cap M_k) - c(R \cap M_{ k + 1 }) \\ &= 0.
\end{align*}\]
Then, as \(Q\) is an \(M_k\)-alternating path, we have \(c_{ M_k }(P) \le c_{ M_k }(Q)\). Using this, we obtain our result \[\begin{align*}
c(M_k \oplus P) &= c(M_k) + c_{M_k} (P) \\ &\le c(M_k) + c_{M_k} (Q) \\ &= c(M_k) + c_{M_k} (Q) + c_{M_k} (R) \\ &= c(M_k) + c_{M_k} (M_k \oplus M_{ k + 1 }) \\ &= c(M_k \oplus (M_k \oplus M_{ k + 1 })) \\ &= c(M_{ k + 1 }).
\end{align*}\]

Implementing this algorithm requires us to find shortest \(c_M\)-weighted aternating paths. Assuming \(G\) is bipartite, we can construct \(G_M\) and reduce the problem to finding the minimum-cost path in \(G_M\) from \(L \cap F\) to \(R \cap F\). The cost for a directed edge \((u, v)\) are just given by the cost for its undirected counterpart, \(c_M (u, v)\).
Note that as edges may have positive and negative costs, the appropriate algorithm to use here is the Bellman-Ford algorithm. However, Bellman-Ford to successfully solve the min-cost path problem, we require that \(G_M\) contains no negative-cost cycles.

Lemma 10 
Suppose \(M\) is the minimum-cost matching of size \(|M|\) in \(G\). Then there are no negative-cost cycles in \(G_M\).


Proof. 
Note that if \(C\) is a cycle in \(G_M\) then \(C\) is an \(M\)-alternating cycle. All alternating cycles have even length. Thus, \(M \oplus C\) is a matching with the same cardinality as \(M\). Consequently, \[\begin{align*}
c(M) \le c(M \oplus C) = c(M) + c_M(C) \implies 0 \le c_M(C).
\end{align*}\]

So, we can find the min-cost incremental paths via Bellman-Ford. The runtime of Bellman-Ford is \(\mathcal{O}(mn)\). There are \(n/2\) iterations and so, the overall runtime of our min-cost perfect matching algorithm becomes \(\mathcal{O}(mn^2)\).


We now present an alternative approach to minimum-cost matching that borrows from economic intuition. Assume that \(L\) represents a set of people who need to be assigned to do a set of jobs \(R\). For an edge \(e = (u, v)\), the cost \(c_e\) is a cost associated with having person \(u\) do job \(v\). Furthermore, there is a price \(p(u)\) associated with \(u \in U\) that corresponds to a “signing bonus” for \(u\) and a price \(p(v)\) associated with \(v \in V\) that corresponds to the reward associated with doing job \(v\). Then, the net cost of assigning a person \(u\) to do job \(v\) becomes \(p(u) + c_e - p(v)\). This merits a special name.

Definition 11 (Reduced Cost) 
The reduced cost of an edge \(e = (u, v)\) is \[ c^p_e = p(u) + c_e - p(v). \]

The benefit of using reduced costs is that it is “equivalent” to using the costs \(c_e\) we originally cared about.

Lemma 11 
Over the feasible set of perfect matchings, minimizing \(M \mapsto \sum_{e \in M} c^p_e\) is equivalent to minimizing \(M \mapsto \sum_{e \in M} c_e\).


Proof. 
It suffices to show that these two objective are monotone and particularly, just differ by a constant factor. Let \(M\) be a perfect matching then, \[\begin{align*}
\sum_{e \in M} c^p_e &= \sum_{e=(u, v) \in M} (p(u) + c_e - p(v)) \\
&= \sum_{e \in M} c_e + \sum_{e = (u, v)} p(u) - \sum_{e = (u, v)} p(v) \end{align*}\] Then as \(M\) is a perfect matching, \[\begin{align*}
&= \sum_{e \in M} c_e + \sum_{u \in L} p(u) - \sum_{v \in R} p(v).
\end{align*}\] Finally, note that \(\sum_{u \in L} p(u) - \sum_{v \in R} p(v)\) is constant across all perfect matchings.

The key thing about Lemma 11 is that it actually gives us a family of equivalent optimization problems, parametrized on our choice of the pricing \(p\). What would be a convenient choice for the pricing \(p\) then? First, of all it would be desirable if finding the augmenting path of minimum cost is a shortest-path problem over non-negative weights. This would allow us to use the more efficient Dijkstra’s algorithm over Bellman-Ford! For a matching \(M\), the weighting of the edges on an augmenting path would be, \[\begin{align*}
\Bbb{1} \{e \notin M\} \cdot c^p_e - \Bbb{1} \{e \in M\} \cdot c^p_e.
\end{align*}\]
Thus, it suffices to consider prices such that \(c^p_e \ge 0\) for all edges and \(c^p_e = 0\) for \(e \in M\).
Furthermore, rather than having to rely on Lemma 9, whose proof involved a slightly delicate induction, it would be nice if a convenient choice of pricing \(p\) could easily certify the optimality of our partial-matching \(M\). For this, since we are already assuming \(c_e^p \ge 0\), it suffices to further require \(c_e^p = 0\) for all \(e \in M\).





We formalize these requirements as follows.

Definition 12 (Compatible Prices) 
A pricing of the vertices, \(p: V \to \mathbb{R}\), is said to be a compatible pricing if

for all unmatched vertices \(v \in V\) we have \(p(v) = 0\);
for all edges \(e\) we have \(c_e^p \ge 0\);
for all edges \(e \in M\) we have \(c_e^p = 0\).

title: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Definition 1 (Matching) 
A matching in an undireted graph is an edge set such that every vertex belongs to either one (matched vertex) or \(\emptyset\) (free vertex) edges of the matching.

Maximum Matching Problem. Given a graph \(G\), find a matching with as many edges as possible.
We start by considering a natural question: given a graph \(G\) and a suboptimal matching \(M\), how should we improve it? Answering this leads to a natural iterative mechanism for producing the maximum matching.
We start by introducing structures in the graph that correspond to ways in which we may alter our matching.

Definition 2 (Alternating Component) 
An \(M\)-alternating component is an edge set that forms a connected subgraph of \(G\) of maximum degree \(2\), in which every degree-\(2\) vertex belongs to exactly one edge of \(M\).

A connected subgraph of \(G\) of maximum degree \(2\) must be either a cycle or a path. It is a cycle iff every vertex has degree \(2\). A proof for this can be furnished by considering the longest path in the subgraph.

Definition 3 (\(M\)-Augmenting Path) 
Suppose \(G\) is a graph and \(M\) is a matching. Then, an \(M\)-augmenting path in \(G\) is a path \(P\) in \(G\) that starts and ends at free vertices and alternates between edges in \(M\) and not in \(M\).

The following are some easy but useful properties of an \(M\)-augmenting path.

Lemma 1 (Properties of \(M\)-Augmenting Paths) 
Let \(P\) be an \(M\)-augmenting path. Then

\(P\) has odd length;
\(|P \backslash M| = |M \cap P| + 1.\)



Proof. 

Let \(P = v_0 v_1 \dots v_k\). Then \(v_i v_{ i + 1 } \in M\) iff \(i \equiv 1 \; (\mathrm{mod} \; 2)\). As \(v_k\) is free, we have \(v_{ k - 1 } v_k \notin M\) which implies \((k - 1) \equiv 0 \; (\mathrm{mod} \; 2)\) so that \(\ell(P) = k \equiv 1 \; (\mathrm{mod} \; 2)\).
Let \(P = v_0 v_1 \dots v_k\). It suffices to show that \(P' = v_0 v_1 \dots v_{ k - 1 }\) is such that \(|P' \backslash M| = |P' \cap M|\). For this just consider the \(P' \cap M \rightarrow P' \backslash M\) bijection defined by \(v_i v_{ i + 1 } \rightarrow v_{ i - 1 } v_i\).


The following result then demonstrates how the presence of a suitable \(M\)-alternating component allows us to alter our matching. Informally, by suitable, we want the alternating component to “never lose track of already matched vertices”– that is the alternating component can contain a vertex from the matching only if it contains the edge the vertex is matched to too.

Proposition 1 (Augmenting by an \(M\)-Alternating Component) 
Suppose \(C\) is an \(M\)-alternating component such that \(v \in V(M) \cap V(C) \implies v \in V(M \cap C)\). Then, \(M \oplus C\) is a matching such that \[|M \oplus C| = |M| + |C \backslash M| - |M \cap C|.\]


Proof. 
We first show that \(M \oplus C\) is a matching. Consider a vertex \(v \in M \oplus C\). It suffices to prove that \(v\) is adjacent to exactly one edge of \(M \oplus C\). Note that \(M \oplus C = (M \backslash C) \sqcup (C \backslash M)\). Note that \(M \backslash C\) is a matching as \(M\) is a matching. Furthermore, \(C \backslash M\) is a matching since every \(v \in V(C \backslash M)\) is adjacent to exactly one edge in \(C \backslash M\). So, it suffices to show that \(M \backslash C\) and \(C \backslash M\) are vertex disjoint. If \(v \in V(M \backslash C)\) then there is a unique \(e \in M\) such that \(v \in e\). Note that \(e \notin M \cap C\) and so \(v \notin V(C)\).
Thus, \[\begin{align*}
|M \oplus C| &= |(M \backslash C) \sqcup (C \backslash M)| \\ &= |M \backslash C| + |C \backslash M| \\ &= |M| + |C \backslash M| - |M \cap C|.
\end{align*}\]

Consequently, an \(M\)-augmenting path is an alternating component that increases the size of the matching.

Corollary 1 (Augmenting by an \(M\)-Augmenting Path) 
If \(P\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path then \(M \oplus P\) is a matching and \(|M \oplus P| = |M| + 1\). Furthermore, every vertex matched in \(M\) is also matched in \(M \oplus P\).


Proof. 
Note that if \(v \in V(P) \cap V(M)\) then by definition of an \(M\)-augmenting path \(v\) must be an interior vertex that is adjacent to an edge in \(M \cap P\). Thus, \(M \oplus P\) is a matching. Furthermore, as \(|P \backslash M| = |M \cap P| + 1\) we have \(|M \oplus P| = |M| + 1\).
Now, we show \(V(M) \subseteq V(M \oplus P)\). Suppose \(v \in M\). Note that if \(v \notin P\), then clearly \(v \in M \backslash P \subseteq M \oplus P\). Otherwise, \(v \in P\) and as \(v\) is not \(M\)-free, it must be an interior vertex that is adjacent to an edge in \(P \backslash M\) which implies \(v \in P \backslash M \subseteq M \oplus P\).

In fact, \(M\)-alternating components completely characterize the maximum matching problem.

Lemma 2 (Changes in Matching I) 
If \(M\) and \(M'\) are matchings in \(G\) then \(M \oplus M'\) is a union of \(M\)-alternating components.


Proof. 
Every \(v \in M \oplus M'\) has degree \(\in \{1, 2\}\) as every vertex has degree at most \(1\) in each of \(M, M'\), with degree \(1\) in at least one or the other. Furthermore, a vertex \(v \in M \oplus M'\) can only be adjacent to at most one edge in \(M\) as \(M\) is a matching. Thus, \(M \oplus M'\) is a union of \(M\)-alternating components.


Lemma 3 (Changes in Matching II) 
If \(M\) and \(M'\) are matchings in \(G\) with \(|M| < |M'|\) then \(M \oplus M'\) contains an \(M\)-augmenting path.


Proof. 
\(M \oplus M'\) is a union of \(M\)-alternating components. An \(M\)-alternating component where all vertices have degree-\(2\) must be a cycle. Since the edges must alternate between edges in \(M\) and in \(M'\), the cycle must have an equal number of edges from \(M\) and \(M'\). Since \(|M| < |M'|\) we must then have an \(M\)-alternating component that is a path and contains more edges from \(M'\) than \(M\).

This motivates a family of algorithms for the maximum matching problem.


\begin{algorithm} \caption{Computing a Maximum-Matching} \begin{algorithmic} \State{\textbf{initialize} $M = \emptyset$} \Repeat \State{$P \leftarrow$ \textbf{find} an $M$-augmenting path} \State{$M \leftarrow M \oplus P$} \Until{there is no $M$-augmenting path} \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


This algorithm terminates in at most \(\mathcal{O}(n/2)\) iterations as each iteration increases the size of the matching by \(1\) and a maximum matching has size at most \(n/2\).
Different strategies for finding the \(M\)-augmenting path \(P\) yield different algorithms.

Definition 4 (Bipartite) 
A graph \(G\) is said to be bipartite if there exists a partition \(V(G) = L \sqcup R\) such that every edge has exactly one endpoint in \(L\) and \(R\).

We now present a simple strategy that works when \(G\) is bipartite.

Definition 5 (\(G_M\)) 
Let \(G=(L, R, E)\) be a bipartite graph and \(M\) be a matching. The graph \(G_M\) is defined as the directed graph formed from \(G\) by orienting each edge from \(L\) to \(R\) if it does not belong to \(M\) and from \(L\) to \(R\), otherwise.


Lemma 4 
Let \(M\) be a matching in a bipartite graph \(G\) and \(F\) be the set of free vertices. The \(M\)-augmenting paths are in one-to-one correspondence with directed paths from \(L \cap F\) to \(R \cap F\) in \(G_M\).


Proof. 
Let \(P\) be a directed path from \(L \cap F\) to \(R \cap F\) in \(G_M\). First, its endpoints are free with respect to \(M\). Since \(G_M\) is bipartite, its edges alternate from edges \(L \to R\) and edges \(R \to L\). That is, the edges alternate from edges in \(M\) and not in \(M\). Thus, the undirected edge set corresponding to \(P\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path.
Next, let \(P\) be an augmenting path. Note that \(P\) has odd length, and hence, its endpoints are on opposite sides of the partition \((L, R)\). Since its endpoints are also free, it suffices to show that \(P\) corresponds to a directed path in \(G_M\). Note that every interior vertex of \(P\) has exactly one edge in \(M\) and one edge not in \(M\). The former edge corresponds to a directed edge \(R \to L\) and the latter corresponds to a directed edge \(L \to R\). Thus, \(P\) corresponds to a directed path in \(G_M\) from \(L \cap F\) and \(R \cap F\).

This gives us a natural algorithm for maximum-matching in a bipartite graph. We merely build \(G_M\) and find a path from \(L \cap F\) to \(R \cap F\) using BFS/DFS. Building \(G_M\) and performing BFS/DFS both take \(\mathcal{O}(m + n)\) time. We may also assume \(m \ge n/2\); otherwise, the graph contains isolated edges which can be removed in a preprocessing step taking \(\mathcal{ O }(n)\) times. Thus, overall, we get a \(\mathcal{ O }(m n)\) algorithm for maximum-matching in bipartite graphs.

title: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Choosing only one augmenting path at a time is quite wasteful. The Hopcroft-Karp algorithm improves upon this by attempting to find many disjoint augmenting paths in every iteration. We start with the following generalization of Corollary 1 and Lemma 3.
As a brief aside, vertex disjoint may refer to different notions depending on the source.

Definition 6 (Vertex Disjoint) 
A set of subgraphs \(\{G_i\}\) are (externally) vertex-disjoint if they share no vertices. A set of paths \(\{P_i\}\) are said to be internally vertex-disjoint if they share no vertices other than their endpoints.


Lemma 5 (Characterization of Augmentable Matchings) 
If \(G\) is a graph and \(M\) is a matching \(G\) then the following are equivalent for all \(k \in \mathbb{N}\)

there exists a matching \(M'\) with \(|M| + k\) edges;
\(G\) contains \(k\) vertex-disjoint \(M\)-augmenting paths;
there exists a matching \(M'\) such that the edge set \(M \oplus M'\) contains at least \(k\) vertex-disjoint \(M\)-augmenting paths.



Proof. 

\(a. \Rightarrow c.\)

Consider \(M'\) such that \(|M'| = |M| + k\). Note that \(M \oplus M' = (M \backslash M') \sqcup (M' \backslash M)\) with \(|M' \backslash M| = |M \backslash M'| + k\). Every vertex \(v \in M \oplus M'\) has degree \(\in \{1, 2\}\) as every vertex has degree at most \(1\) in each of \(M\), \(M'\) and degree \(1\) in at least one of \(M\), \(M'\). Thus, \(M \oplus M'\) must be a union of vertex-disjoint paths and cycles.
As \(M\) and \(M'\) are matchings, each vertex of degree \(2\) in \(M \oplus M'\) is adjacent to exactly one edge from \(M\) and one edge from \(M'\). Since a cycle can be alternating only if it has even length, it has an equal number of edges from \(M\) and \(M'\). Since \(|M' \backslash M| = |M \backslash M'| + k\), there must be at least \(k\)-many \(M\)-alternating paths in \(M \oplus M'\).

\(c. \Rightarrow b.\)

This is immediate by noting that \(M \oplus M' \subseteq E(G)\).

\(b. \Rightarrow a.\)

It suffices to show that if \(P\) and \(P'\) are vertex disjoint \(M\)-augmenting paths then \(P'\) is also a \((M \oplus P)\)-augmenting path. As \(P\) and \(P'\) are vertex-disjoint, they are edge disjoint too. Since endpoints of \(P'\) aren’t adjacent to edges in \(M\) or \(P\), they will be free with respect to \(M \oplus P\) too. Next, any edge of \(M \cap P' \subseteq M \\ P\) is still in \(M \oplus P\). Furthermore, any edge of \(P' \backslash M\) isn’t contained in \(M\) or \(P\) and hence, isn’t an edge in \(M \oplus P\). Thus, \(P'\) is \((M \oplus P)\)-alternating.

Again, we shall assume \(G\) is bipartite. As always, we start with some helpful definitions to frame our algorithm.

Definition 7 (BFS Levels) 
In the graph \(G_M\), define \(L_0, L_1, ..., L_\infty\) to be the levels in a breadth-first traversal rooted at \(L \cap F\). That is,
\[\begin{align*}
L_0 = & L \cap F, \\ L_{i + 1} = &\text{ all vertices } v \notin \bigcup_{ k = 0 }^i L_k \text{ s.t. } G_M \\ &\text{ contains an edge from } L_i \text{ to } v, \\ L_\infty = &\text{ all vertices} v \notin \bigcup_{k = 1}^n L_k.
\end{align*}\]


Definition 8 (Advancing and Retreating Edges) 
An edge \(e = (u, v) \in G_M\) is an advancing edge if \(u \in L_i\) and \(v \in L_{i + 1}\). Otherwise, we call it a retreating edge. A path composed entirely of advancing edges is called an advancing path.

The following lemma then somewhat clarifies the importance of advancing edges.

Lemma 6 
If \(e = (u, v)\) is an advancing edge we must have \(d(v) > d(u) \Rightarrow d(v) = d(u) + 1\). Consequently, an \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\) is an advancing path if and only if it is a shortest \(s\)-\(t\) path.


Proof. 
By definition, if \(e\) is an edge going from \(L_i\) to \(L_j\) for \(j > i\), then we must have \(j = i + 1\). Furthermore, \(L_i\) consists of all vertices that are at a distance of \(i\) from \(L_0\).


Definition 9 (Blocking Set) 
A blocking set of \(M\)-augmenting paths is a maximal (under set-inclusion) set of vertex-disjoint advancing \(M\)-augmenting paths.



\begin{algorithm} \caption{Hopcroft-Karp Algorithm} \begin{algorithmic} \State{\textbf{initialize} $M = \emptyset$} \Repeat \State{$\{P_i\} \leftarrow$ \textbf{find} a blocking set of $M$-augmenting paths} \State{$M \leftarrow M \oplus P_1 \oplus \dots P_k$} \Until{there is no $M$-augmenting path} \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


As before, we know that this algorithm terminates in at most \(n/2\) iterations as each iteration increases the cardinality of \(M\) by at least \(1\). To obtain a superior bound, we need to also integrate an alternative measure of progress. Particularly, we shall show that the length of the shortest augmenting path is strictly increasing every iteration. Intuitively, this occurs because augmenting by a path reverses the orientation of all its edges and hence, any future \(s\)-\(t\) path taking these edges must be longer than the shortest \(s\)-\(t\) paths available prior.

Lemma 7 (Increasing Augmenting Path Lengths) 
If \(M_t\) and \(M_{ t + 1 }\) are the matchings in two consecutive iterations of the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm, the length of the shortest \(M_{ t + 1 }\)-augmenting path is strictly greater than the length of the shortest \(M_t\)-augmenting path.

Our strategy will be to “follow” along a path \(P\) in \(G_{M_{t + 1}}\) while keeping track of the distances as we would in \(G_{M_t}\)! Note that the undirected edge structure of both \(G_{M_t}\) and \(G_{M_{t + 1}}\) are identical, the only distinction lie in the orientation of an edge and the BFS layers. The latter is really a consequence of the former: the availibility of directed edges is what changes the shortest path. Furthermore, the notion of advancing and retreating edges help us compare the path \(P\) in \(G_{M_{t + 1}}\) to the shortest paths in \(G_{M_t}\).

Proof. 
Let \(L_0, L_1, \dots,\) denote the BFS layers of \(G_{ M_t }\) and suppose \(d \in \mathbb{N}\) is minimal such that \(L_d\) intersects \(R \cap F\). Furthermore, suppose \(P = u_0 u_1 \dots u_j\) is a shortest \(M_{ t + 1 }\)-augmenting path. Note that \(u_0, u_j\) must be free with respect to \(M_t\) as once a vertex is matched, it remains matched after augementation too. Below \(d(\cdot)\) denotes the distance in \(G_{ M_t }\) from \(L \cap F\). Edges \((u_i, u_{ i + 1 })\) were either:

advancing edges in \(G_{M_t}\) whose orientation is reversed in \(G_{M_{t + 1}}\) (because \((u_{i + 1}, u_i)\) belonged to a blocking set \(\mathcal{ P }\)) \[ d(u_{ i }) = d(u_{ i + 1 }) + 1, \]
advancing edges in \(G_{M_t}\) whose orientation is preserved in \(G_{M_{t + 1}}\) \[ d(u_{ i + 1 }) = d(u_i) + 1, \]
reversing edges in \(G_{M_t}\) \[ d(u_{ i + 1 }) < d(u_i). \] Thus, in all cases we have \(d(u_{ i + 1 }) \le d(u_i) + 1\). Inductively, \(d \le d(u_j) \le j\).

Note that \(d(u_j) = j\) if and only if \(P\) is an advancing path in \(G_{M_t}\). This implies that \(P\) is edge disjoint from the blocking set of \(M_{t}\)-augmenting paths, \(M_t \oplus M_{ t + 1 }\). Since \(P\) wasn’t used as an augmenting path in iteration \(t\), it must be the case that there exists \(v \in V(M_t \oplus M_{ t + 1 }) \cap V(P)\). Since all vertices in \(V(M_t \oplus M_{t+1})\) are matched in \(M_{t+1}\), vertex \(v\) cannot be an endpoint of \(P\) (which are \(M_{t+1}\)-free). Since \(M_t \oplus M_{t + 1}\) is a blocking set, each vertex therein is adjacent to an edge \(e \in M_{t + 1} \backslash M_t\).
As \(P\) is \(M_{ t + 1 }\)-augmenting and \(v\) is an interior vertex of \(P\), the unique edge of \(M_{ t + 1 }\) adjacent to \(v\), namely \(e\), is contained in \(P\). That is, \(e \in (M_t \backslash M_{ t + 1 }) \cap P\), contradicting the edge-disjointness of \(P\) from \(M_t \oplus M_{ t + 1 }\).
Thus, \(d \le d(u_j) < j\).

Note that as augmenting paths are of odd length, each iteration increases the length of the shortest \(M\)-augmenting path by at least two. Using these measures of progress independently, we get the same bound of \(n/2\) on the number of iterations. Using these two measures in different phases of the algorithm yields a superior bound than using either one alone.

Proposition 2 (Hopcroft-Karp Iterations) 
For any \(t \le n/2\), the number of iterations of Hopcraft-Karp is bounded by \(t + n/2t\).


Proof. 
After \(t\) iterations, the length of the shortest \(M\)-augmenting path is at least \(2 t\). Then let \(k = |M^\star| - |M_t|\). Note that \(M\) must have at least one augmenting path with vertices at most \(n/k\). Hence, \(2 t \le n/k \Rightarrow k \le n/(2t)\). Thus, the runtime is bounded by \(t + k \le t + n/(2t)\).

By the AM-GM inequality, we note that \(\sqrt{ 2 n } \le t + n/2t\) with equality obtained when \(t = \sqrt{n/2}\).

Corollary 2 
Hopcroft-Karp terminates in at most \(\mathcal{ O }(\sqrt{ n })\) iterations.

title: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Minimum-Cost Bipartite Perfect Matching. Given an undirected bipartite graph \(G = (L, R, E)\) together with costs \(c: E \to \mathbb{R}_{ \ge 0 }\) for each edge, find a perfect matching \(M\) that minimizes \(c(M) = \sum_{ e \in M } c(e)\).
Without loss of generality, we shall assume that a perfect matching exists as we have already discussed algorithms capable of detecting this.

Definition 10 (Induced Costs) 
Let \(M\) be a matching. Then \(c: E \to \mathbb{R}_{ \ge 0 }\) induces a cost function \(c_M: E \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \[ c_M (e) = \Bbb{1}\{e \notin M\} \cdot c(e) - \Bbb{1}\{e \in M\} \cdot c(e). \]

This induced cost is natural for \(M\)-augmenting paths due to the following lemma.

Lemma 8 (Costs Under Augmentation) 
If \(P\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path then \[ c(M \oplus P) = c(M) + c_M (P).\]

This motivates a greedy algorithm for our problem. Note that bipartiteness is not required yet.


\begin{algorithm} \caption{Greedy Algorithm for Min-Cost Perfect Matching} \begin{algorithmic} \State{\textbf{initialize} $M = \emptyset$} \While{$M$ is not a perfect matching} \State{$P \leftarrow$ \textbf{find} an $M$-augmenting path minimizing $c_M(\cdot)$} \State{$M \leftarrow M \oplus P$} \EndWhile \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


Correctness follows from a proof by induction showing that at iteration \(t\), we have the minimum-cost matching of cardinality \(t\).

Lemma 9 (Correctness) 
If \(M_k\) is a minimum-cost matching of size \(k\) in \(G\) and \(P\) is an \(M_k\)-augmenting path of minimum incremental cost, then \(M_k \oplus P\) is a minimum-cost matching of size \(k + 1\).


Proof. 
Let \(M_{ k + 1 }\) denote the minimum-cost matching of size \(k + 1\). By definition, we must have \(c(M_{ k + 1 }) \le c(M_k \oplus P)\).
Now, we prove the reverse inequality. \(M_k \oplus M_{ k + 1 }\) is a union of alternating components that must contain at least one \(M_k\)-alternating path \(Q\) as \(|M_{ k + 1 }| = |M_k| + 1\). Let \(R\) denote the union of the remaining alternating components. Note that \(R\) must have the same number of edges in \(M_k\) and in \(M_{ k + 1 }\) since the path \(Q\) already accounts for \(|M_{ k + 1 }| = |M_k| + 1\). So, \(M_k \oplus R\) is a \(k\)-matching and \(M_{ k + 1 } \oplus R\) is a \((k + 1)\)-matching. From this, it is immediate that \(c_{M_k} (R), c_{M_{ k + 1 }}(R) \ge 0\) via \[\begin{align*}
c(M_k) \le c(M_k \oplus R) = c(M_k) + c_{ M_k }(R) \\ c(M_{ k + 1 }) \le c(M_{ k + 1 } \oplus R) = c(M_{ k + 1 }) + c_{ M_{ k + 1 } }(R).
\end{align*}\]
Furthermore, we have \(c_{ M_k }(R) + c_{ M_{ k + 1 } }(R) = 0\) which implies \(c_{ M_k }(R) = c_{ M_{ k + 1 } }(R) = 0\). \[\begin{align*}
c_{ M_k }(R) + c_{ M_{ k + 1 } }(R) &= c(R \backslash M_k) - c(R \cap M_k) + c(R \backslash M_{ k + 1 }) - c(R \cap M_{ k + 1 }) \\ &= c(R \cap M_{ k + 1 }) - c(R \cap M_k) + c(R \cap M_k) - c(R \cap M_{ k + 1 }) \\ &= 0.
\end{align*}\]
Then, as \(Q\) is an \(M_k\)-alternating path, we have \(c_{ M_k }(P) \le c_{ M_k }(Q)\). Using this, we obtain our result \[\begin{align*}
c(M_k \oplus P) &= c(M_k) + c_{M_k} (P) \\ &\le c(M_k) + c_{M_k} (Q) \\ &= c(M_k) + c_{M_k} (Q) + c_{M_k} (R) \\ &= c(M_k) + c_{M_k} (M_k \oplus M_{ k + 1 }) \\ &= c(M_k \oplus (M_k \oplus M_{ k + 1 })) \\ &= c(M_{ k + 1 }).
\end{align*}\]

Implementing this algorithm requires us to find shortest \(c_M\)-weighted aternating paths. Assuming \(G\) is bipartite, we can construct \(G_M\) and reduce the problem to finding the minimum-cost path in \(G_M\) from \(L \cap F\) to \(R \cap F\). The cost for a directed edge \((u, v)\) are just given by the cost for its undirected counterpart, \(c_M (u, v)\).
Note that as edges may have positive and negative costs, the appropriate algorithm to use here is the Bellman-Ford algorithm. However, Bellman-Ford to successfully solve the min-cost path problem, we require that \(G_M\) contains no negative-cost cycles.

Lemma 10 
Suppose \(M\) is the minimum-cost matching of size \(|M|\) in \(G\). Then there are no negative-cost cycles in \(G_M\).


Proof. 
Note that if \(C\) is a cycle in \(G_M\) then \(C\) is an \(M\)-alternating cycle. All alternating cycles have even length. Thus, \(M \oplus C\) is a matching with the same cardinality as \(M\). Consequently, \[\begin{align*}
c(M) \le c(M \oplus C) = c(M) + c_M(C) \implies 0 \le c_M(C).
\end{align*}\]

So, we can find the min-cost incremental paths via Bellman-Ford. The runtime of Bellman-Ford is \(\mathcal{O}(mn)\). There are \(n/2\) iterations and so, the overall runtime of our min-cost perfect matching algorithm becomes \(\mathcal{O}(mn^2)\).


We now present an alternative approach to minimum-cost matching that borrows from economic intuition. Assume that \(L\) represents a set of people who need to be assigned to do a set of jobs \(R\). For an edge \(e = (u, v)\), the cost \(c_e\) is a cost associated with having person \(u\) do job \(v\). Furthermore, there is a price \(p(u)\) associated with \(u \in U\) that corresponds to a “signing bonus” for \(u\) and a price \(p(v)\) associated with \(v \in V\) that corresponds to the reward associated with doing job \(v\). Then, the net cost of assigning a person \(u\) to do job \(v\) becomes \(p(u) + c_e - p(v)\). This merits a special name.

Definition 11 (Reduced Cost) 
The reduced cost of an edge \(e = (u, v)\) is \[ c^p_e = p(u) + c_e - p(v). \]

The benefit of using reduced costs is that it is “equivalent” to using the costs \(c_e\) we originally cared about.

Lemma 11 
Over the feasible set of perfect matchings, minimizing \(M \mapsto \sum_{e \in M} c^p_e\) is equivalent to minimizing \(M \mapsto \sum_{e \in M} c_e\).


Proof. 
It suffices to show that these two objective are monotone and particularly, just differ by a constant factor. Let \(M\) be a perfect matching then, \[\begin{align*}
\sum_{e \in M} c^p_e &= \sum_{e=(u, v) \in M} (p(u) + c_e - p(v)) \\
&= \sum_{e \in M} c_e + \sum_{e = (u, v)} p(u) - \sum_{e = (u, v)} p(v) \end{align*}\] Then as \(M\) is a perfect matching, \[\begin{align*}
&= \sum_{e \in M} c_e + \sum_{u \in L} p(u) - \sum_{v \in R} p(v).
\end{align*}\] Finally, note that \(\sum_{u \in L} p(u) - \sum_{v \in R} p(v)\) is constant across all perfect matchings.

The key thing about Lemma 11 is that it actually gives us a family of equivalent optimization problems, parametrized on our choice of the pricing \(p\). What would be a convenient choice for the pricing \(p\) then? First, of all it would be desirable if finding the augmenting path of minimum cost is a shortest-path problem over non-negative weights. This would allow us to use the more efficient Dijkstra’s algorithm over Bellman-Ford! For a matching \(M\), the weighting of the edges on an augmenting path would be, \[\begin{align*}
\Bbb{1} \{e \notin M\} \cdot c^p_e - \Bbb{1} \{e \in M\} \cdot c^p_e.
\end{align*}\]
Thus, it suffices to consider prices such that \(c^p_e \ge 0\) for all edges and \(c^p_e = 0\) for \(e \in M\).
Furthermore, rather than having to rely on Lemma 9, whose proof involved a slightly delicate induction, it would be nice if a convenient choice of pricing \(p\) could easily certify the optimality of our partial-matching \(M\). For this, since we are already assuming \(c_e^p \ge 0\), it suffices to further require \(c_e^p = 0\) for all \(e \in M\).





We formalize these requirements as follows.

Definition 12 (Compatible Prices) 
A pricing of the vertices, \(p: V \to \mathbb{R}\), is said to be a compatible pricing if

for all unmatched vertices \(v \in V\) we have \(p(v) = 0\);
for all edges \(e\) we have \(c_e^p \ge 0\);
for all edges \(e \in M\) we have \(c_e^p = 0\).

title: Probability Theory
text:
These notes on probability emerge from a familiar struggle: the compulsive search for resources that align perfectly with one’s mathematical background and aesthetic sensibilities. Rather than continuing this perhaps utile pursuit, I’ve decided to synthesize my own understanding from the various imperfect sources I’ve encountered.
Drawing loosely on Erdős’s notion of “the Book”—that celestial collection of the most elegant proofs—I imagine these notes as fragments toward some idealized treatment of probability theory. They represent an attempt to distill what resonates most clearly from my reading, organized according to my own developing intuitions about the subject.
The result is necessarily incomplete and reflects my current limitations, but perhaps that’s appropriate for a subject built on uncertainty.

title: Probability Theory
text:
Introduction

Motivation
Informally, the basis of probability theory is the notion of experiments– processes whose outcomes are uncertain to us. As a prototypic example, we may be interested in phenonmenon associated with tossing a fair coin an infinite number of times.
The sample space, \(\Omega\), is the set of all possible outcomes of our experiment. For our prior example, it is suitable to take it to be the space of all \(\{H, T\}\)-valued sequences, \(\Omega = \{ \omega:\mathbb{N} \to \{H, T\}\}\). An event is a subset \(E \subseteq \Omega\) of outcomes. We are interested in computing the probability of an event, i.e. a measure of the likelihood with respect to the level of uncertainty we have.
As a motivating example, consider the event \[E = \{\text{after tossing a coin until tail comes up the total number of tosses is odd}\}.\]
It is easiest to deal with this by appropriately partitioning the event into disjoint subevents. Let \[E_j = \{ \omega: \mathbb{N} \to \{H, T\} \, \mid \, \omega(1) = \dots = \omega(2j) = H, \omega(2j + 1) = T\}.\]
Then,
\[\begin{align*}
E = \bigsqcup_{j = 0}^\infty E_j \implies \Pr[E] = \sum_{j = 0}^\infty \Pr[E_j] = \sum_{j = 0}^\infty \frac{1}{2^{2j + 1}} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j = 0}^\infty \frac{1}{4^j} = \frac{2}{3}.
\end{align*}\]
There are certain assumptions implicit in what may appear to be an unassuming calculation. Particularly, it was crucial for us to allow ourselves to consider representing events as a countable disjoint union of other events. Furthermore, we assumed that probability behaves in a countably additive manner. Our intuition says that when events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, their probabilities should sum to the probability of their union.
In practice, finite relative frequencies, which is often taken as an emperical measurement of probability, supports the claim of at least finite additivity. There is also the subjective interpretation of probability that may be used to motivate finite additivity.
Such a Dutch book argument can also be extended to the countably infinite case. Though, such an argument requires us to develop a bit of the countably additive theory so we defer it until then.
Make no mistake, the choice of countable additivity or even finite additivity is not a logical necessity but rather a normative choice in our axiomatization–there is no deeper ground truth from which to derive it, only our intuition (and some foresight, credit to a 100 or so years of modern probability) about what properties a reasonable theory of uncertainty ought to possess. We end this section with the most popular of such axiomatizations, consistent with our discussion above.

Definition 1 (Kolmogrov Axioms) 
A probability space is a triple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), with sample space \(\Omega\), event space \(\mathcal{F}\) and a probability measure \(P\), satisfying

\(P(E) \in \mathbb{R}, \, P(E) \ge 0. \quad \forall E \in \mathcal{F},\)
\(P(\Omega) = 1\),
For any countable sequence of disjoint sets, \(\{E_i\}\), we have \[\Pr \left(\bigcup_{i = 1}^\infty E_i\right) = \sum_{i = 1}^\infty \Pr (E_i).\]




A Curious Paradox
The Kolmogrov Axioms require us to assign probabilities on events in \(\mathcal{F}\) as opposed to any possible subset of \(\Omega\). One of the most fundamental probability spaces we may be interested in is the uniform probability space on \(\Omega = [0, 1]\), where for \(a \le b\), we would want \(\Pr([a, b]) = b - a\). Without delving into formalizing this probability space, our point here is that it may be of natural interest to consider probability spaces with properties in addition to those mandated by the Kolmogrov Axioms; for example, translation-invariance. Here is where our problems begin.

Proposition 1 (Imposibility on \([0, 1]\)) 
Let \(\Omega = [0, 1]\). Then, there is no translation-invariant probability measure \(\Pr: 2^\Omega \to [0, 1]\).

Similar ideas give us negative theorems for other spaces too. As an example, consider the following.

Proposition 2 (Impossibility on the Circle) 
Let \(\Omega = \{z \in \mathbb{C} \, \mid \, |z| = 1\}\) be the unit circle. Then there is no rotation-invariant probability measure \(\Pr: 2^\Omega \to [0, 1]\).



\(\sigma\)-Fields
The Kolmogrov Axioms suggest some natural structures for \(\mathcal{F}\). The first axiom necessitates \(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}\). Furthermore, by finite additivity, there is a natural way of assigning a measure to \(A^c\) if \(A \in \mathcal{F}\). \[ 1 = \Pr(\Omega) = \Pr(A \cup A^c) = \Pr(A) + \Pr(A^c) \implies \Pr(A^c) = 1 - \Pr(A). \] That is, it would be desirable for \(\mathcal{F}\) to be closed under complements too. Similarly, the third axiom also suggest that \(\mathcal{F}\) be closed under countable unions.

Definition 2 (\(\sigma\)-Field) 
A collection \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) is a \(\sigma\)-field if

\(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}\);
If \(E \in \mathcal{F}\), then \(E^c \in \mathcal{F}\);
If \(\{E_j\}\) is a countable set of events in \(\mathcal{F}\), then \(\bigcup_{j = 1}^\infty E_j \in \mathcal{F}\).


\(\sigma\)-fields are closed under intersection, which allows us to conveniently talk about the smallest \(\sigma\)-field containing any old family of sets we may be naturally interested in.

Lemma 1 (Closure Under Intersection) 
If \(I\) is any index set and \(\{\mathcal{F}_i \, \mid \, i \in I\}\) are \(\sigma\)-fields over \(\Omega\), then \(\bigcap_{i \in I} \mathcal{F}_i\) is a \(\sigma\)-field.


Proposition 3 (Smallest \(\sigma\)-Field) 
Let \(\mathcal{E} \in 2^\Omega\) be any collection of subsets of \(\Omega\). There is a unique smallest \(\sigma\)-field, \(\sigma(\mathcal{E})\), that contains \(\mathcal{E}\). It is called the \(\sigma\)-field generated by \(\mathcal{E}\).


Lemma 2 (Comparing Generated \(\sigma\)-Fields) 
Let \(\mathcal{E}_1, \mathcal{E}_2 \in 2^\Omega\). Then \(\sigma(\mathcal{E}_1) = \sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\) if and only if \(\mathcal{E}_1 \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_2)\) and \(\mathcal{E}_2 \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{E}_1)\).

When working over a topological space, it is often convenient for the measure to be compatible with the underlying topology; especially with respect to being able to assign a measure to open and closed sets.

Definition 3 (Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra) 
Let \(X\) be a topological space. The Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, \(\mathcal{B}(X)\), is the \(\sigma\)-field generated by the open subsets in \(X\). Events in \(\mathcal{B}(X)\) are called Borel sets.

In practice, constructing a measure over \(\sigma\)-fields directly becomes quite difficult. It will be more useful to first construct finitely-additive measures which we then extend appropriately to the full generality required by the Kolmogrov Axioms.

Definition 4 (Field) 
A collection \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) is a field if

\(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}\);
If \(E \in \mathcal{F}\), then \(E^c \in \mathcal{F}\);
If \(E_1, \dots, E_n \in \mathcal{F}\), then \(\bigcup_{j = 1}^n E_j \in \mathcal{F}\).


Again, motivated by a desire to play nice with the underlying topology, we draw special interest to the following family.

Definition 5 (Borel Field) 
The Borel field, denoted \(\mathcal{B}_{(\,]}(\mathbb{R})\), is the field \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{I}_{(\,]})\) generated by the half-open intervals, \[ \mathcal{I}_{(\,]} = \{(a, b] \, \mid \, -\infty \le a \le b \le \infty\}. \]

First, half-intervals are able to arbitrarily approximate both open and closed intervals; that is, more precisely, any open or closed interval is a countable union of half-open intervals. However, in contrast to the family of just open sets or just closed sets, the set of half-open intervals, \(\mathcal{I}_{(\,]}\), and the field they generate have very nice algebraic properties that are easier to work with.

Definition 6 (Semi-Algebra of Sets) 
A collection \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) is a semi-algebra or elementary class if 1. \(\emptyset \in \mathcal{S}\); 2. If \(A, B \in \mathcal{S}\) then \(A \cap B \in \mathcal{S}\); 3. If \(A \in \mathcal{S}\) then \(A^c\) is a finite disjoint union of elements from \(\mathcal{S}\).


Lemma 3 
The family of half-open intervals, \(\mathcal{I}_{(\,]}\), is a semi-algebra.


Lemma 4 (Semi-algebra Representation) 
If \(\mathcal{S}\) is a semi-algebra over \(\Omega\), then the field \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\) it generates is equal to \[\mathrm{DU}(\mathcal{S}) = \{ \text{all finite disjoint unions of sets from } \mathcal{S} \}.\]



Measures

Definition 7 (Measures) 
A pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) is a measurable space if \(\mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra and a set \(E \in \mathcal{F}\) is called a measurable set. A function \(\mu: \mathcal{F} \to [0, \infty]\) is called a measure if it is countably additive. The triple \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is then called a measure space.
If \(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\), we say \(\mu\) is a finite measure.
If \(\Omega = \bigcup_{i = 1}^\infty A_i\) with \(A_i \in \mathcal{F}\) and \(\mu(A_i) < \infty\) then \(\mu\) is a \(\sigma\)-finite measure.
If \(\mu(\Omega) = 1\), we say \(\mu\) is a probability measure and \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is a probability space.


Lemma 5 (New Measures from Old) 
Fix a measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\). If \(\mu\) is a measure, so is \(\alpha \mu\) for any \(\alpha \ge 0\). If \(\{\mu_j\}_{j \in \mathbb{N}}\) is a countable set of measures then \(\mu = \sum_{j \in \mathbb{N}} \mu_j\) is a measure too.


Proposition 4 (Decomposing \(\sigma\)-Finite Premeasure Space to Finite Premeasure Spaces) 
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite premeasure space. That is, there exists a sequence \(\{A_n\}\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), such that \[\Omega = \bigcup_{n = 1}^\infty A_n\] with all \(\mu(A_n) < \infty\). Take \(\Omega_1 = A_1, \Omega_n = A_n \backslash A_{n - 1}\). Furthermore, \(\mu(\Omega_n) \le \mu(A_n) < \infty\), \(\Omega = \bigsqcup_{n = 1}^\infty \Omega_n\). Define \(\mu_n: \mathcal{A} \to [0, \infty)\) by \(\mu_n(A) = \mu(A \cap \Omega_n)\). Then, \((\Omega_n, \mathcal{A}, \mu_n)\) is a finite premeasure space.


Definition 8 (Increasing, Decreasing Families) 
We write \(A_i \uparrow A\) to mean that \(A_i \subseteq A_{i + 1}\) and \(A = \bigcup_{i = 1}^\infty A_i\). Similarly, we write \(A_i \downarrow A\) to mean that \(A_i \supseteq A_{i + 1}\) and \(A = \bigcap_{i = 1}^\infty A_i\).


Proposition 5 (prperties of Measure) 
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) be a measure space. Then,

If \(E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(E_1 \subseteq E_2\) then \(\mu(E_1) \le \mu(E_2)\) (montonicity);
Suppose \(\{E_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}\) is a countable sequence of measurable sets. Then \(\mu \left(\bigcup_{i = 1}^\infty E_i\right) \le \sum_{i = 1}^\infty \mu(E_i)\) (countable subadditivity);
Suppose \(E_i \uparrow E\). Then \(\mu \left(E\right) = \lim_{i \to \infty} \mu(E_i)\) (continuity from below);
Suppose \(E_i \downarrow E\) and there exist \(j \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(\mu(E_j) < \infty\). Then \(\mu\left(E\right) = \lim_{i \to \infty} \mu(E_i)\) (continuity from above).

Constructing a Premeasure

Premeasure

Definition 9 (Premeasure) 
A pair \((\Omega, \mathcal{A})\) is a premeasurable space if \(\mathcal{A}\) is a field over \(\Omega\). A countably additive function \(\mu: \mathcal{A} \to [0, \infty]\) is a premeasure. If we assume \(\chi\) is only finitely additive, we call it a finitely additive measure.


Proposition 6 (Countable Superadditivity of Finitely Additive Measures) 
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \chi)\) be a finitely additive measure space. If \(\{A_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}\) are disjoint in \(\mathcal{A}\), and \(A = \bigsqcup_{i \in \mathbb{N}} A_i \in \mathcal{A}\) then \[ \chi(A) \ge \sum_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \chi(A_i). \]


Proposition 7 (Extension I: Finitely-Additive Measure from Semialgebra \(\to\) Field) 
Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a semi-algebra over \(\Omega\). Let \(\chi: \mathcal{S} \to [0, \infty]\) be finitely additive. Then \(\chi\) extends to a unique finitely additive measure on \(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S})\), defined by \[ A = \bigsqcup_{i = 1}^n E_i, \, E_i \in \mathcal{S} \implies \chi(A) = \sum_{i = 1}^n \chi(E_i). \]


Proposition 8 (Extension II: Finitely-Additive Meaure on Field \(\to\) Premeasure) 
Let \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq 2^\Omega\) be a semi-algebra. A finitely-additive measure \(\chi: \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{S}) \to [0, \infty]\) is a premeaure if and only if it is countably subadditive on \(\mathcal{S}\), \[ E = \bigsqcup_{j = 1}^\infty E_j \in \mathcal{S} \implies \chi(E) \le \sum_{j = 1}^\infty \chi(E_j). \]


Proposition 9 (Continuity of Premeasures) 
Let \(\mu\) be a finitely additive measure on \((\Omega, \mathcal{A})\). The following are equivalent:

\(\mu\) is a premeasure on \(\mathcal{A}\);
If \(A_n, A \in \mathcal{A}\) and \(A_n \uparrow A\) then \(\mu(A_n) \uparrow \mu(A)\).

Moreover, in the case that \(\mu(\Omega) < \infty\), the following are also equivalent

If \(A_n \downarrow A\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(\mu(A_n) \downarrow \mu(A)\);
If \(A_n \uparrow \Omega\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(\mu(A_n) \uparrow \mu(\Omega)\);
If \(A_n \downarrow \emptyset\) in \(\mathcal{A}\), then \(\mu(A_n) \downarrow 0\).




Stieltjes Premeasure

Proposition 10 (Stieltjes Set Function) 
Let \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a non-decreasing functions. On the semi-algebra, \(\mathcal{I}_{(\,]}\), define \[ \chi_F((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a). \] Furthermore, this is nonnegative and finitely-additive on \(\mathcal{I}_{(\,]}\).


Proposition 11 (Extension III: Stieltjes Set Function \(\to\) Premeasure) 
The set function \(\chi_F\) is a premeasure on \(\mathcal{B}_{(\,]}(\mathbb{R})\) if and only if \(F\) is right-continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\), \[ \lim_{\delta \downarrow 0} F(a + \delta) = F(a). \]


Lemma 6 (Lebesgue Premeasure) 
When \(F(x) = x\), then \(\chi_F\) is a premeasure on \(\mathcal{B}_{(\,]}(\mathbb{R})\) and known as the Lebesgue premeasure.



Outer Measures
Given a premeasurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\), we would like to ideally extend \(\mu\) to a measure \(\overline{\mu}: \sigma(A) \to [0, \infty]\). That is, find a \(\sigma\)-field \(\mathcal{F} \supseteq \sigma(\mathcal{A})\) and a measure \(\overline{\mu}\) on \(\mathcal{F}\) such that \(\overline{\mu} \mid_{\mathcal{A}} = \mu\).

Definition 10 (Caratheodory Extension) 
Let \(\Omega\) be a set and \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^{\Omega}\) such that \(\emptyset, \Omega \in \mathcal{E}\). Let \(\rho: \mathcal{E} \to [0, \infty]\) be such that \(\rho(\emptyset) = 0\). Define the Caratheodory Extension \(\rho^\star: 2^\Omega \to [0, \infty]\), by \[\rho^\star(A) = \inf \left\{\sum_{j = 1}^\infty \rho(E_j) \, \mid \, E_j \in \mathcal{E}, A \subseteq \bigcup_{j = 1}^\infty E_j\right\}. \]


Definition 11 (Outer Measure) 
Let \(\Omega\) be a nonempty set. A function \(\nu: 2^\Omega \to [0, \infty]\) is an outer measure if

\(\nu(\emptyset) = 0\);
\(\nu\) is monotone, \(A \subseteq B \implies \nu(A) \le \nu(B)\);
\(\nu\) is countably subadditive, \(\nu\left(\bigcup_{n = 1}^\infty A_n\right) \le \sum_{n = 1}^\infty \nu(A_n).\)



Lemma 7 (Premeasure, Outer Measure, Measure) 
If \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) is a premeasure space and \((\Omega, \sigma(\mathcal{A}), \nu)\) is a measure space extending it, then \(\nu \le \mu^\star\), on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\).


Proposition 12 (Premeasure, Outer Measure) 
If \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \chi)\) is a finitely-additive measure space, then \(\chi^\star \le \chi\) on \(\mathcal{A}\). Furthermore, \(\chi^\star = \chi\) on \(\mathcal{A}\) if and only if \(\chi\) is a premeasure.

title: Probability Theory
text:
Constructing the Measure
There are a few approaches to extending a premeasure to a measure. The standard approach takes the followin shape:

Define \[ \mathcal{M}_\mu = \{ E \subseteq \Omega \, \mid \, \mu^\star(T) = \mu^\star(T \cap E) + \mu^\star(T \cap E^c), \forall T \subseteq \Omega \}. \]
Show that \(\mathcal{M}\) is a \(\sigma\)-field containing \(\mathcal{A}\).
Show \(\mu^\star\) is countably additive on it.

This approach requires some new tools: Monotone Class Theorem or Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) Theorem. Furthermore, it tends to feel a bit too clever and unmotivated!
At least for finite premeasures, we have a more natural approach on the basis of topological ideas.

Define a topology over \(2^\Omega\).
Define \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) to be the closure of \(\mathcal{A}\).
Show that \(\mu: \mathcal{A} \to (0, \infty]\) is sufficiently continuous to extend it to the closure \(\mathcal{A}\).
Use topological tools to show \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) is a \(\sigma\)-field and \(\overline{\mu}\) is a measure such that \(\overline{\mu} = \mu^\star\) on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\).


Extending Finite-Premeasures

Metric Spaces
We start by recalling some metric space theory.

Definition 12 (Pseudometric Spaces) 
A function \(d: X \times X \to [0, \infty]\) is a pseudometric on \(X\) if

\(x = y \implies d(x, y) = 0\);
\(d(x, y) = d(y, x)\) (symmetry);
\(d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)\) (triangle inequality).



Definition 13 (Limit) 
A sequence \(\{x_n\}\) in \(X\) has a limit \(x\) if \[\forall \epsilon > 0. \exists N \in \mathbb{N}. \forall n \ge N. \; d(x_n, x) < \epsilon. \]


Definition 14 (Closure, Closed Set) 
Let \(X\) be a pseudometric space. Given \(V \subseteq X\), the closure \(\overline{V}\) is the set of limits of sequences in \(V\). A set \(V \subseteq X\) is closed if \(\overline{V} = V\).


Definition 15 (Lipschitz) 
Let \(X\) be a pseudometric space. A function \(f: X \to \mathbb{R}\) is Lipschitz if there exists \(K \in (0, \infty)\) such that for all \(x, y \in X\) we have \(|f(x) - f(y)| \le K \cdot d(x, y)\).


Proposition 13 (Lipschitz Extensions) 
If \(f: V \to \mathbb{R}\) is Lipschitz on a nonempty \(V \subseteq X\), then there is a unique Lipschitz extension \(\overline{f}: \overline{V} \to \mathbb{R}\) with the same Lipschitz constant.

Now, we metrize \(2^\Omega\).

Definition 16 (Outer Pseudometric) 
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeaure space and \(\mu^\star: 2^\Omega \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) be the Caratheodory outer measure. Then, we define \(d_\mu: 2^\Omega \times 2^\Omega \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) by \(d_\mu(E, F) = \mu^\star (E \Delta F)\).


Proposition 14 (Outer Pseudometric) 
\(d_\mu\) is a pseudometric on \(2^\Omega\).


Proposition 15 (Properties of the Pseudometric)  



\(\forall A, B \in 2^\Omega. \; d_\mu(A, B) = d_\mu(A^c, B^c)\);
\(\forall\) sequences \(\{A_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}, \{B\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\) in \(2^\Omega\). Then,

\(d_\mu(\bigcup_{n = 1}^\infty A_n, \bigcup_{n = 1}^\infty B_n) \le \sum_{n = 1}^\infty d_\mu(A_n, B_n)\);
\(d_\mu(\bigcap_{n = 1}^\infty A_n, \bigcap_{n = 1}^\infty B_n) \le \sum_{n = 1}^\infty d_\mu (A_n, B_n)\).




Lemma 8 (Outer Pseudometric: Continuity from Below) 
If \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) is a finite premeasure space and \(A_n \in \mathcal{A}\) with \(A_n \uparrow A\), then \(d_\mu(A_n, A) = \mu^\star(A) - \mu(A_n) \to 0\).



Closure in the Pseudometric

Lemma 9 (Closure, Convergence from Below) 
If \(A_n \in \mathcal{A}\) and \(A_n \uparrow A\), then \(A \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).


Definition 17 (Countable Union Family) 
Given \(\mathcal{E} \subseteq 2^\Omega\), \(\mathcal{E}_\sigma = \{\text{countable unions of elements of } \mathcal{E}\}\).


Proposition 16 (Closure, \(\sigma\)-Field) 
If \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) is a finite premeasure space, then

\(\overline{A_\sigma} = \overline{A}\);
the closure \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\) of the field \(\mathcal{A}\) in the pseudometric space \((2^\Omega, d_\mu)\) is a \(\sigma\)-field.



Proposition 17 (Lipschitz Extension of \(\mu\)) 
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space. Then \(\mu\) extends to a unique Lip-\(1\) function \(\overline{\mu}: \overline{A} \to [0, \infty]\). Furthermore, \(\overline{\mu} = \mu^\star\) on \(A_\sigma\).


Proposition 18 (Characterizing Closure) 
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space. For \(B \in 2^\Omega\), the following are equivalent.

\(B \in \overline{A}\)
\(\forall \epsilon > 0. \exists C \in A_{\sigma}\) such that \(B \subseteq C\) and \(\mu^\star(C \backslash B) = d_\mu(B, C) < \epsilon\).



Proposition 19 (Equality of Extension on Closure) 
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space. Then \(\overline{\mu} = \mu^\star\) on \(\overline{\mathcal{A}}\).



Constructing the Measure

Proposition 20 (Existence of Measure) 
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a finite premeasure space. Then, \(\overline{\mu}: \overline{\mathcal{A}} \to [0, \mu(\Omega)]\) is a measure.


Proposition 21 (Uniqueness of Measure) 
If \(\mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-field with \(\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{F} \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}\) and \(\nu\) is a measure on \(\mathcal{F}\) with \(\nu\mid_{\mathcal{A}} = \mu\), the \(\nu = \overline{\mu}\mid_{\mathcal{F}}\).


Proposition 22 (Existence and Uniqueness for \(\sigma\)-Finite Measure Spaces) 
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite premeasure space. Then, \(\overline{\mu} = \sum_{n = 1}^\infty \overline{\mu_n}\) is the unique measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\) extending \(\mu\).


Proposition 23 
Let \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite premeasure space.

\(\overline{\mu} = \mu^\star\) on \(\sigma(\mathcal{A})\);
If \(B \in \sigma(\mathcal{A})\) and \(\epsilon > 0\), \(\exists C \in \mathcal{A}_\sigma\) such that \(B \subseteq C\) and \(\overline{\mu}(C \backslash B) < \epsilon\).
If \(\overline{\mu}(B) < \infty\), \(\exists A \in \mathcal{A}\) such that \(\overline{\mu}(A \Delta B) < \epsilon\).





The Standard Approach

Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) Systems

Definition 18 (\(\lambda\)-System) 
A collection \(\Lambda \subseteq 2^\Omega\) is a \(\lambda\)-system over \(\Omega\) if

\(\emptyset \in \Lambda\);
\(A, B \in \Lambda\), with \(A \subseteq B \implies B \backslash A \in \Lambda\);
\(A_i \in \Lambda\) and \(A_i \uparrow A \implies A \in \Lambda\).



Lemma 10 (Closure Under Intersection) 
If \(I\) is any index set and \(\{\Lambda_i \, \mid \, i \in I\}\) are \(\lambda\)-systems then \(\bigcap_{i \in I} \Lambda_i\) is also a \(\lambda\)-system.


Definition 19 
Let \(\mathcal{E} \in 2^\Omega\) be any collection of subsets of \(\Omega\). There is a unique smallest \(\lambda\)-field, \(\sigma(\mathcal{E})\), that contains \(\mathcal{E}\). It is called the \(\sigma\)-field generated by \(\mathcal{E}\).


Definition 20 (\(\pi\)-System) 
A collection \(\Pi \subseteq 2^\Omega\) is a \(\pi\)-system over \(\Omega\) if \(A, B \in \Pi \implies A \cap B \in \Pi\).


Lemma 11 (\(\sigma\)-Fields = \(\pi\)-Systems \(+\) \(\lambda\)-Systems) 
A collection \(\mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra if and only if it is both a \(\pi\)-system and \(\lambda\)-system.


Lemma 12 (\(\lambda\)-System Generated By \(\pi\)-System) 
Let \(\Pi\) be a \(\pi\)-system over \(\Omega\). Then, \(\lambda(\Pi)\) is a \(\sigma\)-field over \(\Omega\).


Proposition 24 (Dynkin’s \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) Theorem) 
If \(\Pi\) is a \(\pi\)-system and \(\Lambda\) is a \(\lambda\)-system that contains \(\Pi\) then \(\sigma(\Pi) \subseteq \Lambda\).

Measures on \(\mathbb{R}\)

Radon Measure

Definition 21 (Radon Measure on \(\mathbb{R}\)) 
A Borel measure \((\mathbb{R}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}), \mu)\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) is called a Radon measure if forall \(a < b \in \mathbb{R}\) we have \(\mu((a, b]) < \infty\).


Proposition 25 (Characterizing Radon Measures on \(\mathbb{R}\)) 
If \(\mu\) is a Radon measure on \(\mathbb{R}\), then there exists a non-decreasing right-continuous function \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), unique up to additive constants, such that for \(-\infty \le a \le b \le \infty\) we have \[\mu((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a).\]


Definition 22 (Cumulative Distribution Functions) 
Let \(\mu\) be a Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb{R}\). Then the cumulative distribution function (cdf) of \(\mu\) is the function \(F_\mu: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \[F_\mu(x) = \mu((-\infty, x]).\]


Proposition 26 (Characterizing Radon Measures on \(\mathbb{R}\)) 
Any right-continuous, non-decreasing function \(F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) satisfying \[\lim_{x \to -\infty} F(x) = 0, \lim_{x \to +\infty} F(x) = 1\] is the cdf of a unique Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb{R}\).



Lebesgue Measure

Definition 23 (Lebesgue Measure) 
The Radon measure on \(\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(\lambda((a, b]) = b - a\) for \(-\infty < a \le b < \infty\) is called the Lebesgue measure.


Proposition 27 (Translation Invariance of the Lebesgue Measure) 
The Lebesgue measure, \(\lambda\), is the unique translation invariant Borel measure such that \(\lambda((0, 1]) = 1\). If \(\mu\) is any other translation invariant Borel measure, then \(\mu = \alpha \lambda\) for some \(\alpha \ge 0\).


Definition 24 (Null Set) 
In a measure space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), a measurable set \(N \in \mathcal{F}\) is a null set if \(\mu(N) = 0\).


Lemma 13 
If \(X \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) is countable, then \(\lambda(X) = 0\).


Definition 25 (Cantor Set) 
Define
\[\begin{align*}
\mathcal{C}_0 &= [0, 1], \\
\mathcal{C}_{n + 1} &= \frac{\mathcal{C}_n}{3} \cup \left(\frac{2}{3} + \frac{\mathcal{C}_n}{3}\right).
\end{align*}\]
Then, the Cantor set is defined as
\[ \mathcal{C} = \bigcap_{n = 0}^\infty \mathcal{C}_n. \]


Lemma 14 
If \(\mathcal C\) is the Cantor set then \(\lambda(\mathcal{C}) = 0\).


Definition 26 (Null Completion) 
A measure space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is called (null) complete if, for every \(N \in \mathcal{F}\) with \(\mu(N) = 0\), every subset \(\Lambda \subseteq N\) is in \(\mathcal{F}\).


Proposition 28 (Completion of Measure Space) 
For any measurable space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\), there is an extension \(\widetilde{\mathcal{F}} \supseteq \mathcal{F}\), \(\widetilde{\mu}\mid_{\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}}\) such that \((\Omega, \mathcal{\widetilde{F}}, \widetilde{\mu})\) is complete.

Often, the Lebesgue measure implies a particularly large \(\sigma\)-field, \[\begin{align*}
\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} = \{E \subseteq \mathbb{R} \, \mid \, \forall \lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}. \lambda^\star(A) = \lambda^\star(A \cap E) + \lambda^\star(A \cap E^c)\}.
\end{align*}\]
In fact, we have already encountered this.

Proposition 29 
In a finite premeasure space \((\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \mu)\), we have \(\mathcal{M}_\mu = \overline{\mathcal{A}}\).

In practice, we will not be using \(\mathcal{M}\). For us, the Lebesgue measure is pretty much a Borel measure. Worst case, we may possibly need to complete the Borel \(\sigma\)-field in some applications.

title: 3.1.B Dynamic Programming
text:
The problem with the recursive implementation of Fibonacci was that we would redundantly recompute known values. Memoization (derived from the word memo, not a play on memorization) fixes this flaw by explicitly storing computed values in a table and performing a look up in the table before making recursive calls.

fib_tbl = [0, 1]
def fib_memo(n):
    if len(fib_tbl) <= n:
        fib_tbl.extend([None] * (n - len(fib_tbl) + 1))
   
    if fib_tbl[n] is not None:
       return fib_tbl[n]
    fib_tbl[n] = fib_memo(n-1) + fib_memo(n-2)
   
    return fib_tbl[n]

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import random
import time
def compare_sorts_plot():
    def insertion_sort(arr):
        arr = arr.copy()
        for i in range(1, len(arr)):
            key = arr[i]
            j = i - 1
            while j >= 0 and arr[j] > key:
                arr[j + 1] = arr[j]
                j -= 1
            arr[j + 1] = key
        return arr

    def merge_sort(arr):
        if len(arr) <= 1:
            return arr.copy()
        
        mid = len(arr) // 2
        left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])
        right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])
        
        result = []
        i = j = 0
        while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
            if left[i] <= right[j]:
                result.append(left[i])
                i += 1
            else:
                result.append(right[j])
                j += 1
        
        result.extend(left[i:])
        result.extend(right[j:])
        return result
    
    def benchmark_sorting():
        sizes = list(range(5, 201, 5))
        insertion_times = []
        merge_times = []
        
        for size in sizes:
            # Create random array
            arr = [random.randint(1, 1000) for _ in range(size)]
            
            # Time insertion sort
            start = time.perf_counter()
            for _ in range(100):  # Multiple runs for better timing
                insertion_sort(arr)
            insertion_time = time.perf_counter() - start
            insertion_times.append(insertion_time)
            
            # Time merge sort
            start = time.perf_counter()
            for _ in range(100):
                merge_sort(arr)
            merge_time = time.perf_counter() - start
            merge_times.append(merge_time)
        
        return sizes, insertion_times, merge_times
    
    # Run benchmark
    print("Benchmarking sorting algorithms...")
    sizes, insertion_times, merge_times = benchmark_sorting()
    
    # Create plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6))
    plt.plot(sizes, insertion_times, 'o-', label='Insertion Sort O(n²)', 
             color='#e74c3c', linewidth=2, markersize=4)
    plt.plot(sizes, merge_times, 's-', label='Merge Sort O(n log n)', 
             color='#3498db', linewidth=2, markersize=4)
    
    # Find crossover point
    crossover = None
    for i in range(len(insertion_times)):
        if merge_times[i] < insertion_times[i]:
            crossover = sizes[i]
            break
    
    if crossover:
        plt.axvline(x=crossover, color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
        plt.text(crossover + 10, max(insertion_times) * 0.8, 
                 f'Crossover ~{crossover}', rotation=90, color='red')
    
    plt.xlabel('Array Size')
    plt.ylabel('Time (seconds)')
    plt.title('Sorting Algorithms: When Does Asymptotic Complexity Matter?')
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    
    print(f"\nResults:")
    print(f"Merge sort becomes faster than insertion sort around size: {crossover}")
    print(f"For small arrays (< {crossover}), insertion sort wins despite being O(n²)!")
    print(f"This shows that constant factors can dominate for practical problem sizes.")
